panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Upper photograph of the same newborn showing a closed/drooping left upper eyelid with the right eye open; the caption and in-text describe left-sided ptosis with the lid opening below the upper eyelid margin, matching the configured finding of unilateral congenital ptosis. Disease attribution is supported by the disease-focused article title (neonatal diagnosis of Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome) plus a specific captioned manifestation. Newborn is described in text, so age_group is child (no infant option). B: Lower photograph of the same newborn, closer view of both eyes, showing persistent left upper eyelid ptosis (reduced palpebral aperture) with a normal-appearing right eye, corresponding to the captioned left-sided ptosis of Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome. No jaw-winking (dynamic retraction on sucking/chewing) is demonstrated in this static image, so only the ptosis finding is tagged.

in_text_mentions: erformed soon after birth, left‐eye ptosis was observed without evidence of edema. Namely, the newborn was hardly able to lift his left eyelid, whose opening was below the upper eyelid margin (Figure 1). Pupils were bilaterally isochoric, isocyclic, and reactive to light. Newborn's general appearance and clinical conditions were otherwise normal. No nervous system anomalies were detected. At 3 days of life, a first ophthalmologist evaluation was performed, and possible congenital ptosis was suspected. The red reflex test was normal. Brain sonography excluded abnormalities.
